title: Sharp pain when I stop biting

patient.name: Daniel Clarke
patient.complaint: Sharp pain in a lower left tooth when I chew, especially when I let go.
patient.opening: Something's not right with a tooth on the lower left. When I chew something hard I get this sudden sharp pain. My last dentist couldn't find anything.

topics.label: When it started
topics.answer: On and off for about two months.

topics.label: Pain on biting
topics.answer: Only when I bite on something hard, like nuts or crusty bread. It's very sharp.

topics.label: Pain on release
topics.answer: Yes, actually, it's worst the moment I let go.

topics.label: Hot and cold
topics.answer: Cold drinks give it a short twinge sometimes, nothing that lasts.

topics.label: Night or spontaneous pain
topics.answer: No, it never hurts on its own.

topics.label: Grinding and habits
topics.answer: My wife says I grind my teeth at night. I also chew ice.

topics.label: Where exactly
topics.answer: Lower left, right at the back. Hard to say which one.

items.question: The bite test isolates the pain to the lower left second molar. Click that tooth.
items.helper: Second molar: two teeth behind the premolars.
items.explain: The lower left second molar (37), a classic site for cracks, especially in people who grind.
items.reveal: 37 has a small restoration and a faint vertical line on the distal marginal ridge. Wear facets on the canines.

items.question: Which tests would help you most now? Select all that apply.
items.explain: Biting on individual cusps reproduces the pain on release, transillumination shows the crack line, and the cold test checks the pulp. Radiographs rarely show cracks.

findings.Bite test on individual cusps: Sharp pain on releasing the bite on the distolingual cusp of 37.
findings.Transillumination: The light stops at a line running across the distal marginal ridge of 37.
findings.Periapical radiograph: Normal. Cracks are usually not visible.

items.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explain: Sharp pain on biting hard things, worst on release, reproduced on one cusp, a crack line on transillumination and a normal radiograph point to a cracked tooth.

items.question: In one or two sentences, justify your diagnosis.
items.expected: The pain is sharp, on biting hard food and worst on release, it is reproduced on one cusp with the bite test, transillumination shows a crack line, and the pulp responds normally with a normal radiograph.

items.question: What is the best management?
options: Protect the cusps with a crown or onlay, and monitor the pulp
answer: Protect the cusps with a crown or onlay, and monitor the pulp
items.explain: Cuspal coverage holds the crack together and stops it spreading. Root canal treatment is only needed if pulpitis develops. A night guard helps with the grinding.

items.question: Daniel asks why his last dentist couldn't find anything. What do you say?
items.expected: Cracks are often too fine to see on an X-ray, and only show with special tests like biting on each cusp or shining a light through the tooth. We will protect the tooth with a crown to stop the crack growing, and a night guard will help with the grinding.

teachingPoints: Sharp pain on release of biting is the hallmark of a cracked tooth.
Cracks rarely show on radiographs: use the bite test and transillumination.
Cover the cusps early to stop the crack from spreading into the pulp or root.
